title: Krishna Visits Trivakra and Grants Her a Boon
story:
There was one house in Mathura that Krishna had not yet entered — the house of the woman whose crooked back he had straightened on his first morning in the city. She was called Trivakra, and though her body had been made straight, her heart had been bent toward him ever since that first meeting. The old texts call her the Sairandhri, the serving woman, and they say Krishna knew her longing — the love that burned in her and would not let her rest.

So, one day, he went to her. He took Uddhava with him, and the two of them walked through the streets of Mathura to the house of the woman who had once offered him perfume. Her home was rich, furnished with splendid things, arranged with care for the one she hoped would come. When she saw him approaching her door, she rose from her seat at once, flustered, the calm of her day scattered in a moment. Uddhava, honored for his goodness, sat down on the ground, touching the seat that was offered, leaving the place of honor for his lord.

Then Trivakra prepared herself as one prepares for a festival. She bathed, anointed her skin with fragrant oils, dressed in fine silk and ornaments, wove garlands into her hair, and set out betel and sweet drinks and everything her house could offer. She took Krishna by the hand — his hand adorned with bangles — and drew him close, shy at the newness of his nearness, trembling at what she hardly dared to hope.

And then she embraced him. She pressed him to her breast with both arms, held him as though she would not let him go, and in that embrace her long torment ended. The verses say she had been burning with love for so long that the ache had become her constant companion; and now, holding the blissful form before her, she let the fire at last burn out. She had obtained what the whole world calls hard to obtain — the lord of liberation himself, standing in her small house, letting her hold him.

When she could speak, she asked only one thing: "Stay with me, beloved, for a few days. That is all I ask." She did not ask for wealth, or power, or a place in his court. She asked for his company, for a few days of his presence in the house she had arranged for him.

Krishna, who honors those who honor him, gave her the boon she wished for. He stayed. And when he left, he returned to his own abode, having honored her devotion in the way that mattered most to her — by giving her himself. The serving woman of Mathura, the once-bent Trivakra, had worshipped the lord of all lords, and her worship had not been in vain.
reflection: Trivakra asks for nothing but a few days of Krishna's company, and that is the boon he grants. The story is striking because her longing is not rebuked or spiritualized away — it is met, gently and completely, as devotion that takes the form of love and is answered in kind.
tradition_note: This is the later visit to Trivakra, described in Bhagavata 10.48; her first meeting with Krishna, when he straightened her back, is told in its own episode (10.42).
next_story_tease: Years later, an old classmate from the gurukula would arrive at Dwaraka carrying memories of those student days.
hero_scene: Trivakra, in silk and garlands, embracing Krishna with both arms in her richly furnished house in Mathura, while Uddhava sits on the ground nearby, her long-held longing dissolving into quiet joy.
visual_elements: a love that has found rest
